DOC.EP: EC.02.01.01 The hospital manages safety and security risks. EP 3. The hospital takes action to minimize or eliminate identified safety and security risks in the physical environment.
DOC.FINDING: During unit surveys the following safety issues were identified: 1. OR staff were not familiar with the process to shut-off O2 during a fire or who is responsible. 2. The electrical panel (no. 13B-1) breakers located in the closet on the nursing unit was not completely labeled.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Staff must be educated on the organizations policy for oxygen shut-off during a fire. ? The identified panel components must be labeled to indicate what areas are served by specific breakers. EP 10. When a security incident occurs, the hospital follows its identified procedures.
DOC.FINDING: During site visit at the Fort Smith CBOC, the staff were asked to activate panic alarm for Behavior Health treatment areas. Two staff members activated the portable alarms and indicated that the alarm was silent and would alert security staff. However, on activation the portable device started to beep and security did not respond for some time. Front reception staff stated that they did not call security because they thought it was a drill.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must provide safe alerting system. The system must be tested monthly and provide silent alerting system for BH staff.

DOC.EP: EC.02.01.03 The hospital prohibits smoking except in specific circumstances. EP 1. The hospital develops a written policy prohibiting smoking in all buildings. Exceptions for patients in specific circumstances are defined.
DOC.FINDING: During the survey, several patients were observed smoking on the ground of the facility. The organizations smoke policy states that no smoking is allowed and doesn’t define how and when patients are given permission to smoking.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The policy must detail the process for granting smoking privileges to patients. The organization must change policy to reflect this process.

DOC.EP: EC.02.02.01 The hospital manages risks related to hazardous materials and waste. EP 4. The hospital implements its procedures in response to hazardous material and waste spills or exposures.
DOC.FINDING: During interview of employees in the Infusion Center, it was revealed that there had been a spill of chemo fluids. The spill was greater than 5 cc. Staff in the Infusion Center responded as well as EMS personnel. Infusion Center and EMS staff have not been fit-tested on respiratory protection for spill response greater than 5cc of Chemo as recommended in OSHA guidelines.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Response personnel must be fit-tested for appropriate respiratory protection.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.03 The hospital conducts fire drills. EP 2. The hospital conducts fire drills every 12 months from the date of the last drill in all freestanding buildings classified as business occupancies and in which patients are seen or treated. Note: In leased or rented facilities, drills need be conducted only in areas of the building that the hospital occupies.
DOC.FINDING: At Fort Smith CBOC clinic, documentation of a fire drill/event was not completed at least annually.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Fire drills or events must be documented and evaluated for effectiveness. The organization must document an annual fire drill.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.05 The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of fire safety equipment and building features described below. However, if these types of equipment or features exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 10. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every quarter, the hospital inspects all fire department water supply connections. The completion dates of the inspections are documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 9-7.1).
DOC.FINDING: Inspection of the FDC (fire department connection) in front of building no. 1 revealed that the caps were missing.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must ensure that caps are in place on the FDC. EP 11. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every 12 months, the hospital tests fire pumps under flow. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition.
DOC.FINDING: The organization did test its fire pumps annually. However, the collected data was not plotted to compare factory performance.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The annual test data must be compared to the certified performance test curve. The test data must be plotted. Variations in performance (generally 5% or greater) must be further examined. ? The organization must refer to NFPA 25.

DOC.EP: EC.02.04.03 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical equipment. EP 3. The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains non–life-support equipment identified on the medical equipment inventory. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.04.01, EPs 2-4 and PC.02.01.11, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: In the Nuclear Medicine department, two (2) injection infusion devices were out of date for preventative maintenance. The label indicated that inspection was due October 2009. The devices were used for current patients.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must ensure that all equipment in included in the inventory and checked as required.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.03 The hospital has a reliable emergency electrical power source. The hospital provides emergency power for the following (EPs 1-6): EP 2. Exit route and exit sign illumination, as required by the Life Safety Code.
DOC.FINDING: Battery operated lighting was not provided in generator as required by NFPA 110 and 101.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must install battery operated lighting in the portable generator.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.05 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains utility systems. Note: At times, maintenance is performed by an external service. In these cases, hospitals are not required to possess maintenance documentation but must have access to such documentation during survey and as needed. EP 1. The hospital tests utility system components on the inventory before initial use. The completion date of the tests is documented. (See also EC.02.05.01, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: The organization has installed a portable emergency generator. Observation of the generator revealed that battery warmers were not installed as required to provide reliable operation and starting (NFPA 110- for outdoor areas).
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must install a battery warmer on battery assembly for the outdoor emergency generator.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.07 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains emergency power systems. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of emergency power equipment discussed below. However, if these types of equipment exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 1. At 30-day intervals, the hospital performs a functional test of battery-powered lights required for egress for a minimum duration of 30 seconds. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: At the CBOC Fort Smith: Battery operated emergency egress lighting and exit signs were not tested monthly for 30 seconds.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Battery operated components must be tested for operation at least monthly (30 seconds). The organization must complete and document tests. EP 2. Every 12 months, the hospital either performs a functional test of battery-powered lights required for egress for a duration of 1 1/2 hours; or the hospital replaces all batteries every 12 months and, during replacement, performs a random test of 10% of all batteries for 1 1/2 hours. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: At the CBOC Fort Smith: Battery operated emergency egress lighting and exit signs were not tested yearly for 90 minutes.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Battery operated components must be tested for operation at least yearly (90 minutes). The organization must complete and document tests.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.09 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical gas and vacuum systems. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the medical gas and vacuum systems discussed below. However, if a hospital has these types of systems, then the following inspection, testing, and maintenance requirements apply. EP 1. In time frames defined by the hospital, the hospital inspects, tests, and maintains critical components of piped medical gas systems, including master signal panels, area alarms, automatic pressure switches, shutoff valves, flexible connectors, and outlets. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.05.01, EP 3)
DOC.FINDING: The hospitals policy defines testing frequency as annually for oxygen/medical gas outlets and zone shut off valves. Testing records indicate that this testing was not completed annually.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must review NFPA 99 requirements and complete required testing. Testing of medical gas components must be completed as define in the policy.
